bugs.description: Bare-surname candidates resolve to a single confident "Confirm as X" button (not AMBIGUOUS) whenever only one same-surname entity is registered at scan time — even when the passage content clearly belongs to a different, unregistered person.
bugs.repro: Register only "Raymond Payne", bulk-ingest a document containing bare "Payne" in an unrelated (Code Compliance) context, open it in the Review Queue.
bugs.expected: A bare surname match should read as provisional/low-confidence when the investigation is known-incomplete, or the tool should make it obvious that this offer depends on no other same-surname person being registered yet.
bugs.actual: The candidate renders identically to a genuine strong match - one enabled "Confirm as Raymond Payne" button, state UNREVIEWED - with no visual signal that this is a weak, context-free surname match riding on an incomplete roster.
bugs.impact: A rushed reviewer who trusts the single-option UI (rather than reading the snippet) would silently misattribute 7 documents to the wrong person. This is exactly the Marc/Raymond Payne failure mode the project is named after — it is contained by investigator discipline here, not by the system.

bugs.description: No UI-exposed way to re-scan already-ingested documents after registering a new entity, and scanRecordForReview is not idempotent (adds duplicate candidate rows rather than replacing/superseding).
bugs.repro: Register entity A, ingest documents, register entity B, look for any "rescan" action in the Review Queue.
bugs.expected: Either an automatic or an explicit manual rescan path, and calling it twice on the same record should not duplicate rows.
bugs.actual: No rescan control exists anywhere in the UI; calling the underlying scanRecordForReview function directly (as this test does) adds a second, additive set of candidate rows for the same passage rather than replacing the stale ones.
bugs.impact: An investigation that discovers new people over time (the normal case) accumulates permanently-stale, overconfident candidate rows on already-reviewed documents unless someone manually re-ingests, which is not a realistic workflow for a live case.

bugs.description: Ask Sources requires EVERY extracted search term to literally appear in a document (AND-based substring match in searchInvestigation()), and extractSearchTerms()'s stopword list is incomplete (misses inflections like "mentioning" vs. stopworded "mention/mentions/mentioned", and filler words like "every", "connected", "involving", "appears", "repeatedly", "payments", "changed", "reviewed") - so realistic full-sentence investigator questions silently return zero results even when the underlying content unambiguously exists.
bugs.repro: With Raymond Payne genuinely mentioned in multiple ingested documents, ask "Show me every record mentioning Raymond Payne." via Ask Sources.
bugs.expected: The real, present mentions of Raymond Payne should surface, the same way the equivalent short query "Raymond Payne" already does (verified working, 9+ results for comparable short queries in this same investigation).
bugs.actual: extractSearchTerms leaves in "every" and "mentioning" (not in the stopword list), searchInvestigation then requires ALL of ["every","mentioning","raymond","payne"] to literally appear in a document - no real document contains the literal word "every" or "mentioning" next to this content, so the AND match fails and zero results are returned. Reproduced identically for all 12 of the brief's own example questions (all in full-sentence/question form) - genuinely resolved (not a timeout, confirmed via a 60s diagnostic ceiling), consistently zero results - while short noun-phrase queries ("Holt Construction", "Riverwalk Redevelopment Fund grant") reliably succeed in the same investigation.
bugs.impact: This is the single largest capability gap found in this test: Ask Sources, the project's primary conversational entry point, cannot answer any of the natural, full-sentence questions an investigator would actually type - it only works if the investigator already knows to type bare keyword phrases instead. Every one of the brief's own §12 example questions fails for this reason.
